hints: Look at the electron arrangements of nitrogen and oxygen, not just their positions in Period 2.
Nitrogen is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^3$ with three unpaired p electrons, while oxygen is $1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$ with one paired p orbital.
Think about how two electrons sharing the same small p orbital interact, and what that does to the energy needed to remove one of them.
walkthrough:
**Write the electron configurations**

Great start is to write out what we actually have. Both atoms are in Period 2, so the outer electron is removed from the 2p subshell.

$$\text{N}: 1s^2 2s^2 2p_x^1 2p_y^1 2p_z^1$$
$$\text{O}: 1s^2 2s^2 2p_x^2 2p_y^1 2p_z^1$$

**Spot the key difference**

Nitrogen has a half-filled p subshell with one electron in each orbital. That arrangement is extra stable because electron repulsion is minimised.

Oxygen has to put a fourth p electron into an already occupied orbital, so one orbital now contains a pair.

**Link pairing to ionisation energy**

Two negative electrons in the same small orbital repel each other strongly. This is called spin-pair repulsion.

That repulsion makes it easier to remove one of the paired electrons from oxygen, so less energy is needed despite the higher nuclear charge. That is why the first ionisation energy drops from N to O.

options.A: Incorrect. Both nitrogen and oxygen lose their first electron from the 2p subshell, so there is no change of subshell here. This type of drop happens elsewhere, for example from Be ($2s$) to B ($2p$), but not for N to O.
options.B: This statement is true but it predicts the wrong trend. A greater nuclear charge ($8+$ for O versus $7+$ for N) should attract electrons more strongly and increase ionisation energy. Since oxygen is actually lower, something else must be outweighing nuclear charge.
options.C: Correct. Oxygen has a paired $2p$ electron ($2p^4$) while nitrogen has three unpaired electrons ($2p^3$). Repulsion between the two electrons in the same orbital makes one of them easier to remove, lowering the first ionisation energy of oxygen.
options.D: Incorrect. Both atoms have the same inner shielding from the $1s^2$ electrons, and the $2s^2$ electrons shield to a very similar extent. There is no significant extra shielding in oxygen to explain the drop.
